_note: STARTER catalogue of student misconceptions, tagged onto wrong options via `optionTags` in the quiz banks. Replace or extend with the errors you actually see (homework, exams, discussion sessions). 'description' is phrased as what the student believes; 'correct_idea' is reviewer/briefing text.

misconceptions.description: Photons from stimulated emission have random phase and direction, like spontaneous emission.
misconceptions.correct_idea: A stimulated photon is identical to the stimulating one: same frequency, phase, direction and polarization.

misconceptions.description: Spontaneous emission is triggered by an incident photon, or its rate grows with the incident photon flux, as for stimulated emission.
misconceptions.correct_idea: Spontaneous emission needs no trigger; the rate A is a property of the medium and the transition, independent of the field. Only absorption and stimulated emission scale with the photon flux F.

misconceptions.description: Nonradiative decay emits a photon (for example in a random direction, or into the beam).
misconceptions.correct_idea: Nonradiative decay emits no photon; the energy goes to the surroundings as heat (collisions, phonons) and adds nothing to the photon flux.

misconceptions.description: The excited population drops to zero after one or two radiative lifetimes.
misconceptions.correct_idea: N2(t) = N2(0) exp(-t/tau_sp) never reaches zero at a finite time; a fraction 1/e (about 37%) remains after one lifetime and about 14% after two.

misconceptions.description: Absorption and stimulated emission have different (or unrelated) cross-sections.
misconceptions.correct_idea: For non-degenerate levels sigma12 = sigma21 = sigma (with degeneracies g1 sigma12 = g2 sigma21); whether a beam is absorbed or amplified is decided by the populations.

misconceptions.description: The roles of the levels are swapped: absorption starts from (or depopulates) the excited state, and stimulated emission acts on the ground state.
misconceptions.correct_idea: Absorption removes atoms from level 1 and raises them to level 2; stimulated emission removes atoms from level 2.

misconceptions.description: Strong enough pumping can produce population inversion in a two-level system.
misconceptions.correct_idea: Optical pumping of a two-level system can at best equalize the populations (transparency); inversion needs a 3- or 4-level scheme.

misconceptions.description: Inversion fails in a two-level system because spontaneous emission empties the excited level faster than the pump can fill it.
misconceptions.correct_idea: The limit is that absorption and stimulated emission balance at equal populations (transparency), however strong the pump; the speed of spontaneous decay is not the reason.

misconceptions.description: In a three-level laser the lower level (the ground state) is empty, so any excited population gives inversion.
misconceptions.correct_idea: In a three-level laser the lower level is the ground state, so inversion needs more than half of the atoms excited (Ne > Ng), i.e. an intense pump. N1 ~ 0 is a four-level property.

misconceptions.description: A four-level laser needs the same strong pumping as a three-level one (ground state depleted, more than half of the atoms excited).
misconceptions.correct_idea: In a four-level scheme the lower laser level empties rapidly, so N1 ~ 0 and any N2 > 0 gives inversion; the ground state need not be depleted.

misconceptions.description: The first laser (ruby) was a four-level system, or four-level lasers came first.
misconceptions.correct_idea: The ruby laser was a three-level system; four-level and quasi-three-level schemes were developed to overcome the high pump requirement.

misconceptions.description: Four-level lasers are more efficient because their upper laser level lives longer.
misconceptions.correct_idea: The advantage is that the lower laser level empties rapidly (N1 ~ 0), not a longer upper-level lifetime.

misconceptions.description: The lifetime hierarchy is reversed: the pumped level should be long-lived (to store the pump energy), or the upper laser level should decay faster than it is filled.
misconceptions.correct_idea: The pumped level must decay quickly to the upper laser level (tau32 << tau2) so that population accumulates there.

misconceptions.description: The quantum defect is measured relative to the laser photon (for example 1064/808 - 1 = 32%).
misconceptions.correct_idea: The quantum-defect fraction is q/(h nu_p) = 1 - lambda_p/lambda_0, about 24% here: it is relative to the pump photon.

misconceptions.description: Population inversion (N2 > N1) alone is enough for laser oscillation; cavity losses do not matter.
misconceptions.correct_idea: Oscillation starts only when the gain compensates all losses, which needs an inversion above the critical value.

misconceptions.description: Amplification only needs N2 > N1; the degeneracy ratio does not matter.
misconceptions.correct_idea: Amplification needs N2 > (g2/g1) N1; for N1 < N2 < (g2/g1) N1 the medium still absorbs.

misconceptions.description: Heating the medium to a high enough temperature produces population inversion.
misconceptions.correct_idea: Boltzmann statistics always favour the lower level; even as T tends to infinity one reaches at best N2 = (g2/g1) N1 (transparency). Inversion needs pumping.

misconceptions.description: The cavity (mirrors) supplies the amplification or the inversion, or the pump supplies the feedback.
misconceptions.correct_idea: The active medium amplifies by stimulated emission, the pump creates the inversion, and the cavity supplies the feedback (and introduces the losses).

misconceptions.description: The medium is crossed only once per round trip in the threshold condition, so the factor 2 is dropped (dNc = gamma/(sigma L)) or the internal loss is counted once.
misconceptions.correct_idea: Per round trip the beam crosses the medium and the internal loss twice: dNc = gamma/(2 sigma L) with gamma = gamma1 + gamma2 + 2 gamma_i.

misconceptions.description: A laser emits exactly one frequency (zero linewidth), so its temporal coherence is perfect.
misconceptions.correct_idea: Real emission has a finite linewidth around nu0, so tau_c is finite; a narrower line is more monochromatic.

misconceptions.description: Spatial and temporal coherence are swapped.
misconceptions.correct_idea: Spatial coherence correlates the field at two points on the wavefront; temporal coherence correlates the field at one point at two times.

misconceptions.description: A broader linewidth means a longer coherence time.
misconceptions.correct_idea: tau_c ~ 1/(delta nu): a narrower line gives a longer coherence time and coherence length.

misconceptions.description: The brightness of a diffraction-limited beam depends on its size (only the area, or only the divergence, is considered).
misconceptions.correct_idea: B = P/lambda^2: a larger waist has a larger area but a proportionally smaller divergence, so the two compensate.

misconceptions.description: The divergence of a Gaussian beam is theta = lambda/w0 (the factor pi is forgotten).
misconceptions.correct_idea: theta = lambda/(pi w0).

misconceptions.description: Doppler broadening is a homogeneous broadening mechanism.
misconceptions.correct_idea: Doppler broadening is inhomogeneous (atoms have different resonance frequencies); natural and collision broadening are homogeneous.

misconceptions.description: Saturating a homogeneously broadened line only depresses the gain near the saturating frequency (a spectral hole).
misconceptions.correct_idea: In a homogeneously broadened medium all atoms respond alike, so the whole gain line saturates uniformly; hole burning is characteristic of inhomogeneous broadening.

misconceptions.description: The rotating-wave approximation is valid for any detuning and any field strength.
misconceptions.correct_idea: It drops the fast counter-rotating term and holds near resonance with moderate coupling (Rabi frequency much smaller than the transition frequency).

misconceptions.description: The RWA keeps the fast (omega + omega0) term and drops the slow near-resonant one.
misconceptions.correct_idea: The fast (omega + omega0) term averages out; the slowly varying (omega - omega0) term is kept.

misconceptions.description: The dipole approximation needs the atom to be comparable to or larger than the wavelength (the size ratio is inverted).
misconceptions.correct_idea: It works because a_B << lambda (k a_B ~ 1e-4), so the field is uniform over the atom.

misconceptions.description: The dipole operator connects states of the same parity, so the diagonal elements survive and the off-diagonal one vanishes.
misconceptions.correct_idea: The dipole operator has odd parity: the diagonal elements vanish (no permanent dipole) while <e|H|g> is nonzero because the parities differ.

misconceptions.description: Both amplitudes change at first order in Omega (for example C_g^(1) = -C_e^(1) to keep the norm).
misconceptions.correct_idea: C_g has only even and C_e only odd powers of Omega, so C_g^(1) = 0; the norm is restored at second order.

misconceptions.description: The system matrix is the product with the first element the ray meets on the left.
misconceptions.correct_idea: M = Mn ... M2 M1: the last element the ray meets is leftmost.

misconceptions.description: A converging thin lens has C = +1/f.
misconceptions.correct_idea: In the standard convention the thin-lens matrix has C = -1/f for a converging lens (f > 0).

misconceptions.description: Matrices of successive elements are added to get the system matrix.
misconceptions.correct_idea: Successive elements combine by matrix multiplication, not addition.

misconceptions.description: Finesse increases with cavity length.
misconceptions.correct_idea: Finesse is set by the mirror reflectivity (and other losses), not by the spacing.

misconceptions.description: The free spectral range increases with cavity length.
misconceptions.correct_idea: FSR = c/(2nL) decreases as L grows.

misconceptions.description: The free spectral range is set by the mirror reflectivity rather than the mirror spacing.
misconceptions.correct_idea: FSR depends only on the optical round-trip length; reflectivity sets the finesse.

misconceptions.description: A two-mirror cavity is stable only if the mirror separation is smaller than the radius of curvature (L < R).
misconceptions.correct_idea: For two equal mirrors the stable range is L < 2R; the confocal case L = R lies inside it, not at its edge.

misconceptions.description: A negative g-parameter means the cavity is unstable.
misconceptions.correct_idea: Stability requires 0 < g1 g2 < 1; individual g values can be negative (two negative g give a positive product).

misconceptions.description: Misremembering the definition of the g-parameter (for example g = L/R, g = 1 + L/R or g = 1 - R/L).
The stability condition involves the sum g1 + g2 rather than the product g1 g2.
misconceptions.correct_idea: Stability is 0 < g1 g2 < 1 (it follows from (A + D)/2 = 2 g1 g2 - 1).

misconceptions.description: Boundary cases (planar g = 1, concentric g = -1, confocal g = 0) count as stable, or as the most stable configurations.
misconceptions.correct_idea: They lie exactly on the stability boundary: marginally stable, which practical resonators avoid.

misconceptions.description: Stability can be decided from the determinant AD - BC of the round-trip matrix.
misconceptions.correct_idea: The determinant is 1 for any round trip in one medium, so it carries no stability information; the trace (A + D)/2 decides.

misconceptions.description: In the (g1, g2) diagram the diagonal g1 = g2 is the stability boundary, or the only stable configurations.
misconceptions.correct_idea: The diagonal marks the symmetric resonators; the stable region is 0 < g1 g2 < 1 on both sides of it.

misconceptions.description: Real and imaginary theta are swapped: imaginary theta (|(A + D)/2| > 1) is taken to give bounded, stable rays.
misconceptions.correct_idea: Real theta (|(A + D)/2| < 1) gives bounded rays; imaginary theta gives exponentially growing rays.

misconceptions.description: The wavefront is most strongly curved at the beam waist.
misconceptions.correct_idea: The wavefront is flat at the waist; its radius of curvature is smallest at z = +/- the Rayleigh range.

misconceptions.description: A higher cavity Q means a shorter photon lifetime.
misconceptions.correct_idea: Q = omega * tau_c, so higher Q means a longer photon lifetime (lower loss).

misconceptions.description: Above threshold the steady-state population inversion keeps increasing with the pump rate.
misconceptions.correct_idea: In steady state the inversion is clamped at the critical value; extra pump power goes into laser output.

misconceptions.description: Spatial hole burning only occurs in ring (travelling-wave) cavities.
misconceptions.correct_idea: It arises in standing-wave (linear) cavities, whose intensity nodes leave gain unsaturated.

misconceptions.description: A longer cavity makes single-mode operation easier.
misconceptions.correct_idea: A shorter cavity has a larger free spectral range, so fewer modes fall within the gain bandwidth.
